ROUGE-L moves by ten points when one library lowercases and the other does not, or when the two tokenize differently. Read the metric setup before you compare, and in your own harness fix one tokenizer and one smoothing rule and pin them with tests.
questions.full:
### The scale

The two BLEU numbers are the same score on two scales. Nothing to debug; write the scale next to every number you publish.

### The tokenizer

The capstone uses one tokenizer for every metric: lowercase the text and keep runs of word characters. Every metric reads the same tokens. Swap the tokenizer and you run a different benchmark. The ten point ROUGE-L gap is what that swap looks like when one side keeps case and the other drops it.

### What else is inside the number

- **BLEU-4** counts modified n-gram precision for n from 1 to 4. The count of each candidate n-gram is clipped at its maximum count in any reference, so a candidate cannot win by repeating one phrase. The brevity penalty lowers the score of a candidate shorter than the reference. Add one smoothing on the counts avoids a log of zero when no 4-gram matches, and stays close to the unsmoothed value on long candidates.
- **ROUGE-L** finds the longest common subsequence. Recall is the subsequence length over the reference length, precision is the same over the candidate length, and the score is their F1.

### What to do in your harness

Write the metrics yourself so a colleague can audit them. Pin them with reference vectors from worked examples, not from a third party library. Test the edge cases: empty prediction, empty reference, no shared tokens, an exact match and a repeated phrase.
questions.followups:
- **Level 2:** Why does clipping matter in BLEU? Expected: a candidate that repeats one matching phrase would inflate n-gram precision; clipping caps the count at the reference count.
- **Level 2:** What does the brevity penalty do? Expected: it lowers the score of a candidate shorter than the reference, so a short output cannot win on precision alone.
- **Level 3:** Why add one to the n-gram counts? Expected: a pair with no matching 4-gram would give a log of zero and a score of zero; smoothing keeps the geometric mean finite and barely moves long candidates.
- **Level 3:** How do you keep your metric numbers comparable across a year of runs? Expected: pin the tokenizer and the smoothing in code, keep reference vectors in tests, and record the metric version with every leaderboard.
questions.wrong:
- "Use the library everyone uses." Two libraries differ by ten points on the same outputs; you still need to know which tokenizer and casing each applied.
- "BLEU is old, drop it." It still backs most published numbers; learn to read it, then layer model based metrics on top.
- "Lowercasing cannot move a score by ten points." The capstone reports that it does for ROUGE-L across two libraries; casing changes which tokens match.

questions.title: Two harnesses, two pass at k formulas
questions.prompt: Two harnesses in the repository compute pass at k. The first takes the empirical pass rate p and returns `1 - (1 - p) ** k`. The second takes the sample count n, the pass count c and k, and returns `1 - C(n - c, k) / C(n, k)`. Read both. When do they agree, when do they differ, and which one goes in the report?
questions.short: The first formula treats every draw as independent with success probability p and is a plug in estimate. The second counts the exact chance that k samples drawn from the n you ran contain at least one pass, and it is the unbiased estimator that code generation benchmarks use. They agree only as n grows large; for the samples you ran, the plug in is lower and noisier, and it extrapolates when k exceeds n. Report the unbiased one with the raw counts next to it.
questions.followups:
- **Level 3:** In the second function, why return one when n minus c is smaller than k? Expected: you cannot pick k failing samples from fewer than k failures, so every k subset contains a pass.
- **Level 3:** Why compute the product in log space? Expected: binomial coefficients overflow for moderate n; the log of the ratio is a short sum of logs.
- **Level 4:** A team ran five samples per task and reports pass at ten. What is wrong? Expected: k exceeds n, so nothing was measured; the second function falls back to whether any sample passed and the first extrapolates.
- **Level 4:** Do the two functions agree on pass at one? Expected: yes; both reduce to c over n when k is one.
questions.wrong:
- "They are the same formula." They agree only as n grows; for the samples you ran, the plug in is lower and noisier.
- "Pass at k is the probability the agent is right." It is the chance that a set of k samples contains at least one pass; without a selector the user still gets one sample.
- "More samples per task raise pass at one." They make the estimate more precise; the value is the per sample pass rate.

questions.title: Error bars for a pass rate and for a mean
questions.prompt: Your eval report shows two kinds of numbers: a pass rate, which is the share of cases that scored 4 or more, and a mean judge score on a 1 to 5 scale. A reviewer asks for error bars on both. Which interval do you use for each, and why not the same one?
questions.short: Use a Wilson interval for the pass rate and a bootstrap interval for the mean score. A pass rate is a proportion, and the Wilson interval stays correct at small samples and near zero or one, where the normal approximation breaks. A mean of ordinal judge scores has no clean closed form, and the bootstrap resamples the scores with replacement and works with any distribution.
questions.full:
### The Wilson interval

```text
center = (p + z^2 / (2n)) / (1 + z^2 / n)
spread = z * sqrt( (p (1 - p) + z^2 / (4n)) / n ) / (1 + z^2 / n)
```

With z at 1.96 for 95 percent. The center moves toward one half when n is small, and the bounds are clamped to zero and one. At 50 cases and 90 percent accuracy it gives 78 to 97 percent. The normal interval would give bounds that can leave the unit range and a width that is wrong at the extremes.

### The bootstrap interval

Resample the n scores with replacement, compute the mean, repeat a thousand times, sort the means and read the percentiles at alpha over two from each end. It assumes only that the sample represents the population. It cannot repair a biased or tiny sample, and it costs compute rather than algebra.

### Comparing two runs

Neither interval compares two systems by itself. For two prompt versions that ran on the same cases, build the interval on the paired per case difference, by bootstrap over cases or a paired test. Two separate intervals that overlap do not prove equality, and two that do not overlap are not needed to prove a difference.
questions.followups:
- **Level 3:** What goes wrong with a plus or minus one standard error interval on a proportion? Expected: at small n or near zero or one it gives bounds outside the unit range and the wrong width; Wilson corrects both.
- **Level 3:** What does a bootstrap assume? Expected: that the sample represents the population; it needs no distribution shape, but it cannot fix a biased or tiny sample.
- **Level 4:** Two prompt versions ran on the same 200 cases. Which interval decides? Expected: an interval on the paired per case difference; two overlapping intervals do not prove equality.
questions.wrong:
- "Plus or minus the standard error is fine." The normal interval fails at small samples and extreme proportions, exactly where releases are decided.
- "Bootstrap works for the pass rate too, so use it everywhere." It works, but Wilson is closed form, cheap and built for proportions; keep the code auditable.
- "Overlapping intervals mean no difference." Two separate intervals can overlap while the paired difference excludes zero; compare the difference.
